title: The Resurrection and the Life: Lazarus Raised
summary: Jesus hears that his friend Lazarus is sick but waits two days, and by the time he reaches Bethany Lazarus has been dead four days. He tells Martha, “I am the resurrection and the life,” weeps with Mary and the mourners, and calls Lazarus out of the tomb. The sign leads many to believe, but it also drives the council under the high priest Caiaphas to plan Jesus' death, and Caiaphas unknowingly prophesies that one man will die for the people.
story: This is the last and greatest of the signs in the first half of John (the seventh, for readers who count the walking on the sea among them), and it is the hinge of the Gospel. Every earlier sign pointed to Jesus as the giver of life; this one shows him defeating death itself. It is also the event that directly causes his arrest. In the other Gospels the cleansing of the temple is the last straw for the authorities; in John, the decision to kill Jesus follows the raising of Lazarus. So the chapter makes a painful exchange plain: Jesus gives life to Lazarus, and it costs him his own. From here the story moves toward the final Passover, which is near (11:55).
historical:
Bethany was a village on the eastern slope of the Mount of Olives, a little under two miles from Jerusalem (11:18). Going there meant returning to Judea, where Jesus had just escaped stoning (10:31), which is why Thomas expects to die with him (11:16). The Sanhedrin (11:47) was the Jewish high council in Jerusalem, made up of chief priests, elders, and scribes, many of them Pharisees, and presided over by the high priest. Under Roman rule it governed internal Jewish affairs, but it held its authority at Rome's pleasure. Caiaphas, called high priest “that year” (11:49, 51), held the office from about AD 18 to 36, an unusually long tenure that suggests he worked well with the Roman governors, including Pontius Pilate. John's phrase probably means high priest in that fateful year. An ossuary (a limestone box for bones) inscribed with a form of the name Caiaphas was found in Jerusalem in 1990, and many scholars think it belonged to his family.

The council's fear was realistic. Rome did not tolerate popular movements around a would-be king, and the leaders worried that a crowd following Jesus would bring the legions and cost them their place, meaning the temple, and their nation (11:48). The irony is sharp for John's readers: Rome did destroy the temple in AD 70. As elsewhere, the Jews in the chapter are a varied group. Many come to comfort the sisters, many believe (11:45), and some report to the Pharisees; the plot is the work of the council, not a people. The raising of Lazarus is not told in the other three Gospels. Some think they focused on Jesus' Galilean ministry and passed over it; others suggest early reticence because Lazarus himself became a target (12:10); critical scholars have often treated it as John's theological composition. The chapter is written with the detail of eyewitness memory, and John presents it as history.
cultural:
Jewish burial happened quickly, usually on the day of death, since bodies decayed fast in the heat. The body was washed, wrapped in linen strips with spices, and laid in a family tomb, often a cave cut into rock and closed with a stone. Mourning lasted seven days, during which friends and neighbors came to sit with the family, and wailing was expected; many visitors had come to console Martha and Mary. The detail that Lazarus had been dead four days matters. Later rabbinic writings record a belief that the soul lingered near the body for three days, and after that decay made death beyond doubt. Martha's blunt warning about the smell (11:39) makes the same point.

Martha's confession that her brother will rise “in the resurrection at the last day” (11:24) reflects the belief of the Pharisees and many ordinary Jews that God would raise the dead at the end of the age (Daniel 12:2). The Sadducees denied it. Jesus doesn't correct Martha's hope but draws it into himself: the resurrection is not only an event at the end but a person present now.
literary: The chapter is carefully paced. The delay (11:6) builds tension, and a sequence of encounters follows: with the disciples, with Martha, with Mary, and at the tomb. Martha and Mary greet Jesus with the same words, “Lord, if You had been here, my brother would not have died” (11:21, 32), but Jesus answers each differently: Martha with teaching and a question, Mary with tears. Misunderstanding drives the dialogue, as the disciples take sleep literally. The fifth of the seven “I am” sayings with an image, “I am the resurrection and the life” (11:25), stands at the center. The raising itself is told in a few lines, and the chapter closes with an ironic prophecy on the lips of an enemy. The grave clothes in 11:44 prepare the reader for Jesus' own tomb, where the linen will be left behind (20:6-7).

outline.t: News of Lazarus' illness and the deliberate delay
Martha: I am the resurrection and the life
Mary and the mourners; Jesus weeps
The council plots, and Caiaphas prophesies
Jesus withdraws as Passover draws near

doctrines.note: Christian hope is resurrection hope. Jesus promises that whoever believes in him “will live, even though he dies” (11:25). Lazarus was raised to die again; his raising is a sign pointing to the final resurrection that Jesus' own rising will begin.
Jesus knows he will raise Lazarus, yet he weeps (11:35) and is deeply moved. Grief is not unbelief. The Son of God enters human sorrow and stands with those who mourn before he acts.

Caiaphas says it is better that one man die for the people (11:50). John sees in the cynical calculation a true prophecy: Jesus would die for the nation and for the scattered children of God, to gather them into one (11:51-52).

words.note: Anastasis, resurrection, literally a standing up again. Martha uses it of the general resurrection at the last day. Jesus takes the same word as a name for himself (11:25). The New Testament uses it for bodily resurrection, not the survival of the soul alone.

Embrimaomai, to be deeply moved, used in 11:33 and 11:38. Outside the New Testament it can describe a horse snorting, and elsewhere in the Gospels it means stern warning or indignation (Mark 1:43; 14:5). Many interpreters think it here expresses anger as well as sorrow, perhaps at death itself, the enemy that destroys God's creation, or at the grief and unbelief around him. Others read it more simply as deep emotion. The word keeps Jesus' response from being merely sentimental.

Dakruō, to weep or shed tears, found only here in the New Testament (11:35). It differs from klaiō, the loud wailing of the mourners (11:33). Jesus' weeping is quieter, tears rather than lament, and the shortest verse in most English Bibles carries great weight.

Sumpherō, to be advantageous or better. Caiaphas argues from expediency: it is better for you that one man die (11:50). His words are political calculation, yet John sees God's purpose speaking through them, since Jesus' death is indeed for the good of the people.

christ: The chapter shows Jesus as Lord over death. The prophets had promised that God would open graves and bring his people out (Ezekiel 37:12-13) and that the dead would rise (Isaiah 26:19; Daniel 12:2). Jesus calls a dead man out by name, as he said in 5:28 that all in their graves would hear his voice. At the same time, the chapter shows his full humanity: he loves his friends, he is troubled, and he weeps. John sets the two together deliberately, and the church's confession that Christ is truly God and truly human finds some of its clearest ground here. Above all, the chapter points ahead. The one who raises Lazarus is about to die so that others may live, and his own tomb will soon be empty.

hard.q: If Jesus loved Lazarus, why did he wait two days while his friend died?
hard.a:
The text puts the two facts together deliberately: “Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus. So on hearing that Lazarus was sick, He stayed where He was for two days” (11:5-6). The delay was not indifference. Jesus says the sickness is for the glory of God (11:4) and that he is glad for the disciples' sake that he was not there, so that they may believe (11:15). He intended something greater than a healing: a raising that would show him as the resurrection and the life. Some readers note that Lazarus was probably already dead when the messengers arrived, since the trip plus two days adds up to four; on that view the delay changed nothing for Lazarus but made the sign unmistakable.

The hard part remains: the sisters suffered real grief, and both said so. Jesus doesn't rebuke them for it. He weeps with them. The chapter doesn't promise that God's love will always act on our schedule, but it shows that his delays are not absence, and that he grieves in the meantime with those who are grieving.

questions: Martha and Mary both say, “Lord, if You had been here, my brother would not have died.” What would it look like to bring that kind of honest disappointment to Jesus?
Jesus asks Martha, “Do you believe this?” What difference does belief in the resurrection make to how you face your own death or the death of someone you love?
Jesus weeps even though he is about to raise Lazarus. What does his grief say about how Christians should grieve?
